articles.title: New Robinsons Sports & Leisure unit to bring global concepts to the Philippines
articles.summary: The new team will is set to shape global concepts and expertise around local interests and lifestyles

items: Robinsons Sports and Leisure (RSL) aims to enhance the quality of life for Filipinos by providing accessible sports, recreation, and entertainment experiences that foster community engagement and personal growth.
The 'glocal' approach combines international sports concepts with local interests, ensuring that facilities and programs are relevant and welcoming to all, from beginners to serious athletes.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

Editor’s note: This press release is sponsored by Robinsons Land Corporation and was handled by BrandRap, the sales and marketing arm of Rappler. No member of the news and editorial team participated in the publishing of this piece.

The hours we remember most are rarely the ones we planned down to the minute. A friendly match stretches into one more game. The last kilometer of a run reveals inner strength we didn’t know we had. Somewhere in a darkened theater, an entire audience holds its breath. And when those moments have passed, we carry something from them back into everyday life: a little more confidence, a deeper connection, the simple pleasure of feeling fully alive.

There is a Filipino word for that renewed energy: sigla. And Robinsons Sports and Leisure (RSL), Robinsons Land’s newest business unit, wants to make room for more of it for every Filipino. By bringing quality sports, recreation and entertainment experiences closer to where Filipinos live, work, shop and stay, RSL hopes to make these hours—our precious “me time”—a little more rewarding by fulfilling its promise, “For a Life That Moves You.”

RSL looks to the world for inspiration and to Filipino communities for direction. Its distinctly “glocal” approach brings international sports and leisure concepts and expertise closer to home, shaping them around local interests and lifestyles. The aim is to make these experiences relevant, accessible, and community-driven, giving Filipinos opportunities to discover something new and make it their own.

“The world is full of exciting ways to play, compete and recharge. We at Robinsons Land want to bring more of these experiences within reach of every Filipino and make them feel right at home here,” said Ramon Rivero, Robinsons Land’s chief strategist and RSL head. “That’s what “glocal” means to us: pairing international expertise with a real understanding of the communities we serve. A first-time player should feel welcome. Someone training seriously should have room to grow. Reeling senses after a night of live entertainment. And everyone should come away with more confidence, connection, and sigla.”
“Glocal” is a portmanteau combining global and local which describes the practice of living with a mindset that spans both worldwide and regional scales.
Robinsons Land’s entry into sports and leisure builds on decades of experience developing places that are woven into Filipino daily life.

“For 46 years, Robinsons Land has built homes, workplaces, malls and hotels around the changing needs of Filipinos,” said Mybelle V. Aragon-GoBio, Robinsons Land president and CEO. “Sports and leisure give us another way to make sure that those developments become a part of every Filipino. We want our destinations to offer meaningful experiences worth making time for, with the quality and consistency that communities have come to expect from us.”

RSL is finding new possibilities within Robinsons Land’s existing developments. Rooftops and open areas can be transformed into courts and recreational spaces, bringing sports and leisure closer to where people already live, work and spend time together. A game after work or a weekend activity with friends can then seamlessly become a natural part of daily life.

Some will come to compete, others to learn, and still others simply for the pleasure of staying active and spending time with friends. RSL hopes to welcome them all, from curious beginners and weekend players to serious athletes and older adults discovering new ways to keep moving.

That spirit of participation will be on display on November 29, when the RSL Run Crew makes its debut at the AIA Rock ’n’ Roll Running Series Manila. Part of an international series that combines road racing with live music and entertainment, the event will bring runners together for a celebration of fitness and camaraderie along Manila’s historic streets.

Another opportunity arrives on December 7 with the public opening of GX Sports at Robinsons Galleria. The facility will feature two pickleball courts and an official HYROX Training Zone under the HYROX Training Club X (HTCx) concept. Equipped with race-standard equipment, a prescribed layout, and structured programming, the zone will help participants prepare for HYROX, the global fitness race combining running and functional workouts.

“The specialized training environment brings an internationally recognized fitness format within reach of Filipino enthusiasts, whether they are preparing for competition or looking for a new challenge,” adds Rivero.

In 2027, three GX Sports In Motion events will offer different ways to participate, giving people more opportunities to meet, compete and enjoy activities together. RSL will also continue developing the programming and partnerships that bring its facilities to life.

blocks.caption: WORLD-CLASS FACILITIES. Helios Beta at Bridgetowne brings world-class pickleball facilities closer to Filipino communities, creating new spaces where recreation, competition, and connection come together

blocks.text: A friendly game and an international tournament begin the same way: someone steps onto the court.

At Bridgetowne, the fast-rising sport will take center stage when Helios Beta hosts the PPA Asia 500 Manila Open 2027. Operated by Kosmas Athletic Ventures Corporation (KAVC), the 14-court facility will bring international tournament action to an estate where residents, workers, and visitors can also make sports part of their everyday lives.

blocks.caption: TOURNAMENT-GRADE. Designed to international standards, Helios’ tournament-grade courts are set to host top-level competition while serving as an everyday destination for players of all skill levels

blocks.text: Bridgetowne’s pickleball offerings will expand further with the development of the separate 25-court Helios Pickleball Center, a joint venture between Robinsons Land and KAVC. International expertise is helping shape the project, with KAVC tapping Johns Design & Consulting, the consultancy of professional pickleball players Collin and Ben Johns, as design consultant. The brothers’ experience competing at venues around the world will help inform the state-of-the-art facility’s planning, design, and events programming.

Beyond Bridgetowne, additional pickleball courts are planned for selected Robinsons malls and offices. Each new location can bring the sport within reach of another community, giving more Filipinos a chance to discover the game, improve their skills, and perhaps turn an occasional match into a weekly tradition.
The thrill of a close match, the magic of a live performance—there are many ways to bring people together. RSL is making room for more of them.

In Cebu, the approximately 1,850-seat NUSTAR Grand Theater is slated to open in 2028, expanding RSL’s offerings into live entertainment and culture. “NUSTAR Grand Theater will be the largest entertainment and cultural venue in the VisMin Region,” shares Rivero. He adds that RSL is looking forward to the venue for the grandest and best live entertainment to hit Philippine shores in the coming months.

Beyond the theater, RSL is exploring an even wider range of leisure possibilities, including sports and golf simulators, padel courts, flexible black-box spaces for entertainment and social activities, and wellness experiences. RSL will pursue these opportunities where demand is clear, the location is suitable and there is a strong potential for repeat participation.

“This deliberate approach supports Robinsons Land’s premiumization strategy, which seeks to make its destinations more distinctive, appealing and rewarding to visit,” says Rivero. This will translate to RSL developing thoughtfully designed facilities, engaging programs and forge specialist partnerships, with consistent high standards of quality, service and safety across locations and offerings shaped by the interests of each community.

The real test will come after opening day. Will people enjoy themselves enough to return? Will a new interest become a lasting passion, or a favorite activity find a regular place in someone’s week? These are the signs that an experience has found its way into people’s lives—and the measure of RSL’s success.

That is the promise behind RSL’s “glocal” vision: bringing the world’s possibilities closer to Filipino communities and giving people the freedom to make those experiences their own. An idea that began halfway around the world can become a favorite pastime, a familiar gathering place or a tradition shared among friends.
The game ends, the curtain falls, and everyone makes their way home—with a little more sigla than when they arrived. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Beau Lamarre-Condon allegedly played Taylor Swift’s No Body, No Crime during body disposal, court told
articles.summary:
Friend of accused double murderer tells supreme court that van had lemony smell and blue tarp in back before Bunnings stop

Beau Lamarre-Condon played Taylor Swift’s song No Body, No Crime…

blocks.text: Beau Lamarre-Condon played Taylor Swift’s song No Body, No Crime while attempting to dispose of two corpses, a court has heard.
The NSW supreme court has been told he was driving to Bungonia with a friend when the song was played in the van.
Lamarre-Condon, 31, is accused of fatally shooting Jesse Baird and his partner, Luke Davies, with his police service weapon in Baird’s Paddington home on 19 February 2024.
He has pleaded not guilty to two counts of murder and one charge of aggravated break and enter.

A friend of Lamarre-Condon, known to the court under the pseudonym Elizabeth Kennedy, said she thought she and the officer were going out for lunch when he picked her up on 21 February 2024 – two days after the alleged murders.
He arrived at Kennedy’s home in a white van about 3pm that day, she told the court.
Defence lawyer John Stratton SC on Wednesday suggested Lamarre-Condon told her: “I’m not joking, if you don’t want to help me I completely understand and I won’t be mad”.
He claimed Lamarre-Condon lifted a tarpaulin, which had been stored in the back of the van, and showed Baird’s deceased head.
Stratton said the officer had told her Baird was dead and suggested Kennedy said: “this is like a Taylor Swift song, No Body, No Crime” before playing the song in the car.
She denied Stratton’s suggestions and said he didn’t show her Baird’s body, nor did she choose the song.
“He was the one that put that song on in the car … it’s a very niche song,” she told the court.
“I asked him how he knew it and he said it was from the album, evermore.
“I tried to play a few more songs from the album, evermore, and he didn’t know any of them so it was very weird to me he knew that song.”
Kennedy on Wednesday morning offered her own account of events to the court.
She said she noticed a blue tarp in the back of the van and a lemony smell, like it had just been cleaned.
As Lamarre-Condon took the wheel, the drive got longer and longer, she said.
Every time she asked how much further, he would respond, “just 50 more minutes”. It ended up being a two-hour drive to Goulburn and Bungonia, about 150km away, the court heard.
The van’s windows were open the entire trip and the air-conditioning was on full blast and freezing, Kennedy told the jury.
She said that during the drive he seemed “bubbly” and talked about Swift, who was touring Australia at that time, as well as a Europe trip they were planning together.
They eventually stopped at Bunnings Goulburn, the court heard.

In a statement read to the court on Wednesday morning, a Bunnings sales assistant said he had been approached by two customers that day who claimed they were staying at a friend’s farm in nearby Bungonia and had locked themselves out.
The worker suggested they use an angle grinder.

blocks.caption: A screenshot of Beau Lamarre-Condon captured on CCTV at Bunnings Alexandria in Sydney on 20 February, 2024. Lamarre-Condon has pleaded not guilty to the murders, saying the men were killed in self-defence. Photograph: NSW supreme court/PR HANDOUT

blocks.text: As Lamarre-Condon and Kennedy went to the Bunnings checkout, the officer asked her to pay for an angle grinder and padlock because he did not have cash with him, she said.
The two then drove to Cella Farm in Bungonia and Lamarre-Condon explained he knew the people who owned the property.
When they arrived, he asked her to put garbage bags over the van’s number plates, but she refused, so he did it himself, Kennedy said.
He then cut the padlock off the gate, cutting himself in the process and asked Kennedy to wait there and not turn on her phone.
“He left me there and drove out of sight behind the house where the bigger dam was,” she told the court.
Kennedy began having a panic attack and, when Lamarre-Condon returned 30 or 40 minutes later, he told her to shush and asked if she had called anyone or turned on her phone.
As they began the return journey to Sydney, he asked if they could go back to Bungonia but she said she needed to be home.
Lamarre-Condon was “weird and cryptic” on the trip back, the court heard.
“It seemed like something went wrong and he wouldn’t tell me about it,” Kennedy told the court.
At one point he almost ran over a bird and said, ‘you know I’d never hurt an animal, right?’, Kennedy said.
Lamarre-Condon attempted to call another police officer friend during the drive.
When the friend didn’t pick up, he said: “‘fuck fuck fuck’ and then he sort of panicked and that’s when he started saying, ‘if I’m quiet, I’m not angry, I’m just thinking’”, the court heard.
He told Kennedy he would have to return to Bungonia and that he would be up all night.
She asked why and he said he could not tell her because he did not want to involve her, the court heard.
He then asked if she could buy him a peach Lipton ice tea as he needed caffeine but didn’t drink coffee.
As she entered the service station to purchase the beverage, he also asked her to fuel up the van, but she couldn’t do it because she didn’t know how to drive or fill up a vehicle.
He was “visibly annoyed” before he swore and jumped out of the car. When asked why he did not want to do it, Kennedy told the court he said he did not want to be on camera.
As they left, she noticed the blue tarp was no longer in the back of the van.
The bodies of Baird and Davies were later found in Bungonia.
The defence team claims Baird and Davies were accidentally shot as the accused acted in “self-defence”.
Lamarre-Condon cleaned up the scene and disposed of the bodies afterwards because he “panicked considerably”, Stratton SC has said.
The trial before Justice Natalie Adams continues.

articles.title: A student protest movement has gripped Serbia for two years. This weekend it will try to take power
articles.summary:
Unorthodox campaign is challenging the ruling party’s 12-year reign with a bold democratic experiment

On a cool autumn evening, a team of Serbian student volunteers went canvassing in the…

blocks.text: On a cool autumn evening, a team of Serbian student volunteers went canvassing in the housing estates of Krnjača, a Belgrade suburb. They were equipped with lanyards emblazoned with the word “victory”, a stock list of questions and a mobile app that mapped visited homes and the level of support in each.

The volunteers were part of a mass student movement, Student List, that has rocked Serbia with two years of constant protests. On Sunday, the group will represent the most serious challenge Aleksandar Vučić has faced in his 12 increasingly authoritarian years in power, by putting forward their own candidates in parliamentary elections.
They hope to emulate the defeat of Vučić’s ally, Viktor Orbán, in neighbouring Hungary six months ago, in a domino effect that could bring a democratic resurgence to central Europe.

Opinion polls have varied wildly, but many expert observers say a close race is quite possible, with neither side prepared to accept a loss as a legitimate result, raising the risk of post-election unrest and clashes.

blocks.caption: Student List supporters in Nis hold balloons shaped like the number three, their position on electoral ballots. Photograph: Marko Đurica/Reuters

blocks.text: In order to win, the students’ list of 250 candidates would have to break the mould of Serbian politics, along with Vučić’s grip on the country. He stepped down as president last month, five months before the end of his second and last term in office under the constitution, but only with the aim of extending his hold on power as prime minister at the head of his Serbian Progressive party (SNS).

In the section of the suburb assigned to them, law student Zak Veličković and campaign photographer Danijela Radojković were welcomed with overwhelming support. Apart from a small handful of polite doorstep rejections, from those claiming they had no interest in politics, people seized the opportunity to air their grievances.
Most promised their vote and a large minority offered help: some taxi drivers with flats in the low-rise apartment blocks said they would help ferry voters to the polling stations.
“Turnout is the key,” one said, adding: “Orbán fell with 80%” – a reference to the Hungarian elections in April.
Veličković began each conversation by asking what was the biggest problem in Serbian society, a query that often raised a laugh and replies such as: “How much time do you have?”

Corruption was the most frequent single complaint. On the corruption index run by Transparency International, Serbia ranks far worse than any of its neighbours, as the most corrupt country in Europe bar the dictatorships in Belarus and Russia.

There are frequent allegations of links between the SNS and organised crime, and the Student List’s slogan confronts that widespread perception head on, posing the question: “Serbia or Mafia?” The government denies all accusations and officially claims to be tackling organised crime.

The key local issues in Krnjača were the poor repair of the road bridge linking the suburb and central Belgrade, and the sewage system, which repeatedly fails in heavy rain, despite a personal promise by Vučić, who residents said had visited a few years earlier, to fix the problem.

The economy has been growing in recent years, but there is a widespread opinion that the fruits are not being fairly distributed. Porsche and Land Rover car showrooms have been established in Krnjača but public spaces look neglected. Some of Belgrade’s trams are more than 50 years old.

It was a major infrastructure failure that sparked the student protests – the collapse of a concrete canopy in Novi Sad railway station on 1 November 2024, killing 16 people. Evidence pointed to botched modifications made during refurbishment work, but so far there has been no official finding on the cause, and no official has been held accountable.

blocks.caption: Rescue service workers inspect the collapsed roof at Novi Sad railway station. Photograph: Interior Ministry of Serbia/AP

blocks.text: When Belgrade students blocked a road in a vigil for the victims three weeks after the disaster, they were attacked by a SNS mob and the protest movement went nationwide.

The students initially distanced themselves from opposition parties and avoided any kind of hierarchy or conventional leadership structure. That was partly an ideological choice and partly practical. The SNS and state-run media rule in part through smearing opponents and the student’s collective approach offered fewer targets.

Vučić rose to prominence in the 1990s as a radical nationalist, who supported the policies of Serbian expansion and ethnic cleansing led by Slobodan Milošević, who died of a heart attack in detention in The Hague during his trial on charges of genocide and crimes against humanity committed in Croatia, Bosnia and Kosovo. He served as Milošević’s information minister throughout the Kosovo conflict. As president, Vučić has not emulated his predecessor’s militarism, but he has maintained his nationalist playbook in domestic politics, dismissing the opposition as stooges of unspecified foreign powers.

blocks.caption: Aleksandar Vučić gives a speech at a campaign rally in Novi Sad last week. Photograph: Maxim Konankov/NurPhoto/Shutterstock

blocks.text: So far those well-worn tactics have proved ineffective against the students. A survey published in July by a Serbian pro-democracy group, the Centre for Research, Transparency and Accountability (CRTA) and Stanford University showed significantly more support for the students (45%) than for the SNS (36%), but that was well before Vučić announced his resignation on 27 September and his election machine went into top gear. Other, more recent domestic polls show the SNS in the lead, though the pollsters in question are seen by the opposition as pro-government.

Vučić himself shows signs he is taking the political threat seriously enough to throw himself into the campaign, making 129 live television appearances in August, more than four times the previous month’s total.

“Serbia has been an electoral autocracy and in electoral autocracies only ruling political parties can win,” Raša Nedeljkov, CRTA’s programme director, said. But he added that the status quo was now in jeopardy.

“What we are seeing in the past days, weeks, months, is that strength; the homogeneous government that Vučić used to have is no longer there. He is faced with a completely unorthodox political actor and the toolbox that he has improved over the years since he came to power is no longer effective.”

Unable to crush the students by force, division or denigration, Vučić gambled, announcing his resignation as president on 28 September and calling snap elections, in the apparent hope of catching the students off guard, but they responded by improvising a democratic experiment.

The 250 candidates were mostly nominated by university faculties (there are more than 160 doctorates among them) with a sprinkling of farmers and other professions, and each candidate was subject to approval by plenary sessions of the student protests.
after newsletter promotion

The policy platform has also been decided by plenum, with the result that divisive issues, especially foreign policy, have been played down: the question of future EU membership has been left to a referendum and Kosovo is claimed as an integral part of Serbia.
One of the chosen candidates, Milica Jovanović, an assistant professor at the University of Belgrade, argued the List’s lack of political experience was not necessarily a drawback.

“We are political amateurs, but we are experts,” Jovanović said. “We are people who have led projects, led organisations, led our community, and actually I cannot see that we can do worse than these politicians … The only thing that matters is willingness to improve something, expertise to actually do it and support to do the actual change.”

The Student List is pitted against the political monolith of the SNS, in power for 14 years and with control of the state apparatus. It has accused the foreign ministry of rigging the diaspora vote by keeping polling stations open where support for Vučić is strong, such as the Serbian part of Bosnia, while closing them in parts of North America where the opposition could expect to perform well. The ministry did not respond to a request to comment.

The SNS grip on national media is meanwhile evident everywhere. A CRTA survey in September found that 69% of air time on Serbian television channels was dedicated to the ruling majority. Of the remaining coverage of the opposition, 42% was negative in tone and 53% neutral.

blocks.caption: A billboard with a campaign poster of Aleksandar Vučić in Belgrade. Photograph: Darko Vojinović/AP

blocks.text: The student movement has sought to sidestep government domination of the media by, it says, going door to door, including sending a canvasser “to every village”, in the hope of making inroads into Vučić’s solid base in the Serbian countryside. The outcome could hinge on whether these student emissaries can change rural minds.

No SNS officials responded to a request for comment. Gordana Čomić, a former member of the opposition Democratic party who served as a minister in the SNS government, said the students were exaggerating the extent of their rural campaign and were deluded if they thought they could win.

“They are not in the field. It’s propaganda. They have no clue who their voters are,” Čomić said, predicting that the Student List would win about 80 of the 250 seats in the national assembly and then dissipate.
“They won’t have a clue what’s their role there. How will they work when they don’t want to talk with anyone from the ruling parties? They will just dissolve.”

Radivoje Grujić, a Serbian electoral consultant based in Warsaw, was also sceptical that the Student List could make gains in the countryside and argued the students’ only path to victory would be if the Novi Sad disaster mobilised Serbians who had previously stayed away from politics.

“These people were saying: I’m not involved in politics, and then politics got them killed,” he said. “This definitely triggered a lot of people to get involved and obviously those people will not vote for Vučić. I think that’s the only chance for a change – that reservoir of votes of people who never voted.”
In a close race, other factors are expected to come into play. Minority parties representing ethnic Hungarians, Bosniaks and Albanians could emerge as kingmakers.

Previous elections have seen multiple allegations of various forms of rigging, including vote-buying, voter intimidation and ballot box stuffing, so the Student List is planning to deploy an unprecedented number of opposition monitors on Sunday.

That could in turn raise the prospect of election day clashes. Attacks on opposition representatives by gangs of anonymous, black-clad burly men has been a frequent feature of SNS rule. In the days before the elections, one of those hired thugs has turned whistleblower.

“My role was to lead a group of guys to the riskiest and most critical places, to any gatherings where students or the opposition were on the other side,” Momcilo Marjanovic told the Balkan Investigative Reporting Network, saying that he was covertly paid through a fictitious job at a public utility.
“It was our job, as a last resort of course, to use force, although it often happened not as a last resort.”

Diplomats in Belgrade thought that Vučić’s plans to host a major international event, EXPO 2027, next year, could constrain any violence. If his hold on power is threatened, Vučić also has the option of forcing repeated recounts in the hope that the students’ momentum may eventually dissipate.
The movement is determined that will not happen and has focused its planning in recent weeks on post-election street tactics to defend any victory.
“I think there is a strong feeling of now or never,” Jelena Kleut, an associate professor of media studies, said at a recent demonstration outside the education ministry in Belgrade.
“I think that people have really felt in their skin what the regime is capable of and there is a sense you still need to stay strong because the job is not finished.”

articles.title: Fifth foreign firm pulls out of controversial Israeli cable car project to East Jerusalem
articles.summary:
Rights groups say the planned 1.4km route, which ends at compound run by far-right settler group Elad, will displace Palestinians and reshape the cultural landscape

A fifth foreign…
articles.byline: Lorenzo Tondo and Quique Kierszenbaum in Jerusalem

blocks.text: A fifth foreign company has pulled out of a plan to build a cable car from West to East Jerusalem that threatens to involve the seizure of land and property rights from dozens of Palestinian families along its route, but local authorities insist the scheme is proceeding as planned.

The project appeared to have stalled for four years until late September, just weeks before Israel’s 27 October elections, when the Jerusalem Development Authority (JDA) issued a notice of intent to award a contract without a public tender to ROPES, a cable car engineering consultancy based in South Tyrol, Italy.
However, Stephan Obexer, chief executive of ROPES told the Guardian his company had declined the consultancy work because of another commitment in India.

The 1.4km cable car route, approved by the Israeli government in 2019 and upheld by the high court in 2022, would connect West Jerusalem to a planned 16,000 sq metres tourist complex promoted by Elad, a settler organisation seeking to consolidate Israeli control over Palestinian areas of occupied East Jerusalem.

The Israeli occupation of the Palestinian territories began in 1967 and the Old City and the rest of the eastern half of Jerusalem were fully annexed in 1980, although they are still considered occupied under international law.

According to Emek Shaveh, an Israeli NGO, the JDA had recently accelerated plans for a long-delayed cable car through occupied East Jerusalem, where Israel’s continued presence has been ruled unlawful by the international court of justice, in a project once described by former Jerusalem mayor Nir Barkat as a way for visitors to “understand who is truly the landlord of the city”.

‘‘This project threatens the Palestinian communities and the timeless landscape of Jerusalem’s historic core,’’ said Emek Shaveh in a recent statement. ‘‘It is clear that the project’s central motivation is to consolidate the settlers’ hold in those areas as part of an effort to displace Palestinians from the Historic Basin and reshape Jerusalem’s cultural landscape.’’
The plan comes amid escalating settler violence and efforts to seize Palestinian land across the occupied territories.

At least four foreign companies – three French and one Swiss – have expressed interest in the project, but several have withdrawn over its political sensitivity, according to Haaretz, an Israeli newspaper. In 2015, the French government urged one company not to participate. Another French company, CNA, pulled out less than a year ago, followed more recently by Switzerland’s Histec Engineering.
ROPES did not respond to a request for a written statement or questions about whether legal concerns over the project’s location in occupied East Jerusalem had influenced its decision.
The JDA did not respond to the Guardian’s request for comment.

But a spokesperson for the JDA told Haaretz: “Following the high court of justice’s dismissal of petitions against the project about a year and a half ago, the cable car continues to proceed according to plan and in accordance with the timetables set. Steps to promote the project are subject to the mandatory tenders law, and the tender is expected to be ready for publication in the coming months once its formulation is completed.”

The move has sparked protests from Israeli heritage and environmental groups and Palestinians in Silwan, an East Jerusalem neighbourhood at the foot of the Old City, who warn that the project threatens Palestinian heritage in territory they seek for a future state and would see cable cars passing just metres above their homes.

“The cable car stands in complete contradiction to the historic principle that no large buildings or infrastructure should be built around the Old City,’’ says Alon Arad, an archaeologist and the executive director of Emek Shaveh. ‘‘It is particularly troubling that the Israel Nature and Parks Authority, the body responsible for upholding this principle, is cooperating with the project.

“To understand the political context, one must look at the route: it begins in West Jerusalem and ends at a compound run by the far-right settler organisation Elad Foundation, which stands to benefit from a project costing the state around half a billion shekels. Elad is notorious for using state resources to advance its political agenda in East Jerusalem, taking over Palestinian properties, evicting families and settling Jewish residents in their place.”
The Elad Foundation, which does not appear to be formally involved in the project, did not respond to the Guardian’s request for comment.

blocks.caption: Palestinian women shopping for bread in the Old City of Jerusalem during Ramadan.  Photograph: John Wessels/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: According to rights groups, the cable car project directly threatens about 54 Palestinian homes along its route in the Wadi Hilweh neighbourhood in Silwan, with the expropriation of either land or air rights, and indirectly threatens many others in the vicinity. Israeli authorities have issued 17 expropriation notices covering about 8.7 dunams (2.15 acres) of land along the proposed route, where pylons supporting the cable car would be erected.

“These buildings, home to roughly 450 residents, lie directly beneath the proposed route,” said Sari Kronish, an architect and director of the East Jerusalem department at Bimkom, an Israeli planning rights organisation. “Cable cars would pass as close as four metres above rooftops and near residential windows, violating residents’ privacy and restricting future development. Expropriations of land and homes for support pillars have already been set in motion, leaving residents in a constant state of uncertainty.”
Reached by the Guardian, the Israel Nature and Parks Authority said: “Our involvement was limited to providing feedback on the proposed alternatives.”

Across occupied East Jerusalem, Israeli settlers are increasingly taking over Palestinian properties, while authorities have stepped up demolitions of homes lacking building permits, displacing families. The Mount of Olives, home to some of Christianity’s holiest sites, has also become a target of settler expansion, raising concerns among churches that own land there.

The campaign has intensified since the war in Gaza started in October 2023 amid accelerating land seizures and settlement expansion across the occupied West Bank, where more than 1,100 Palestinians have been killed by Israeli forces or settlers.

blocks.caption: The surge in settler violence includes this week’s attack on European diplomats. Photograph: UGC/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Settler violence has surged during the annual olive harvest. On 16 October, settlers attacked Palestinian villages, burning cars and trees and injuring a Washington Post photographer. The following day, settlers attacked European diplomats, a French mayor and Palestinian olive pickers, injuring three people and damaging a diplomatic vehicle.

articles.title: Firefighters voice growing concerns over water supplies to tackle UK wildfires
articles.summary:
During a summer fire that destroyed homes in Stourbridge, low pressure meant filling a water carrier took 40 minutes

Concerns have been raised about how drought affects the UK’s ability to…

blocks.text: Concerns have been raised about how drought affects the UK’s ability to cope with wildfires after MPs were told firefighters struggled for water supplies during this year’s record summer.
The government has been urged to set out water companies’ statutory responsibilities during major fire incidents to improve the country’s preparedness for the years ahead.

The UK experienced its hottest-ever summer this year, with prolonged dry periods and extreme heat fuelling wildfires across the country. Figures released earlier this month showed a clear upward trend in the number of fires recorded each year.

The chair of the National Fire Chiefs Council (NFFC), Phil Garrigan, told MPs on the environment, food and rural affairs (EFRA) committee that fires developed more quickly because of limited water supplies. He said concerns about water availability had grown during his 37 years in the fire service.
During a wildfire in Stourbridge in the West Midlands that destroyed several homes, replenishing a water carrier took almost 40 minutes because of reduced water pressure.
In tackling a separate wildfire in the New Forest in August, the fire service said maintaining water supply had been a significant challenge.
after newsletter promotion

Fire services take water from mains and open sources such as lakes and rivers. With levels in the latter extremely low as result of the drought, the fire service’s access was restricted. It also faced pressure to limit its use of mains water to avoid shortages for paying customers.

“In summers like this year, we would normally ask for more resources, but those resources aren’t always available and we’re having to wait longer for additional resources or we’re having to find other ways to deal with the fire,” said Dave Swallow, the NFCC’s deputy lead on wildfires.
A survey of UK fire and rescue services in the summer found that 81% of respondents had changed their emergency response plans in areas where access to water was a concern.

The NFCC, which conducted the survey, said growing pressure from climate breakdown, population growth, housing development and emerging infrastructure such as datacentres, was increasing demand on an already stretched water network.

“Firefighters cannot fight fires without water. That sounds obvious, yet our evidence shows four in five fire and rescue services have had to change response plans because of concerns about firefighting water supplies,” Garrigan said in the summer.

As the climate crisis worsens and demand for water increases, the Environment Agency estimates that England’s public water supply could be short by 5bn litres a day by 2055 without urgent action to future-proof resources.

The EFRA committee has called for water for firefighting to be recognised as a critical public safety requirement. It said the government should establish a statutory framework and national protocol setting out water companies’ responsibilities during major fire incidents, including minimum expectations for water supply and pressure, communication and operational coordination with fire and rescue.
The committee also said water companies should be required to assess, test and verify their ability to support firefighting operations.
“Water companies must be relied upon for adequate supply,” the committee chair, Alistair Carmichael of the Scottish Liberal Democrats, said.

A government spokesperson said: “Improving wildfire preparedness is a major government priority. That’s why this week we are holding a summit with government ministers, fire and rescue leaders, land managers and other partners to understand how we can strengthen the response to this increasing risk.”
A government-funded UK wildfire conference is scheduled to take place in Leeds on 10 and 11 November.

articles.title: Eastern Visayas Army commander to youth: Shun West PH Sea lies
articles.summary: TACLOBAN CITY — The Army’s Eastern Visayas commander has urged young people to stay informed about issues affecting the country’s territorial integrity and sovereignty and guard against…

blocks.text: TACLOBAN CITY — The Army’s Eastern Visayas commander has urged young people to stay informed about issues affecting the country’s territorial integrity and sovereignty and guard against disinformation amid renewed tensions between the Philippines and China over the West Philippine Sea.

Brig. Gen. Peter Burgonio, commander of the Army’s 8th Infantry Division based in Catbalogan City, Samar, said the youth have an important role in understanding national security concerns and supporting efforts to protect the country’s territory.
“To our young people, we are facing issues concerning our country’s security and, of course, threats to our territorial integrity and sovereignty,” Burgonio said in an interview.
“I call upon them to join our government in its call for unity, to focus on whatever they are supposed to do, and to actively participate in the effort to defend our country,” he added.

Burgonio urged the youth to educate themselves about developments involving the country’s territorial claims and maritime rights, saying a better understanding of the issues would help them avoid being misled by false or misleading information.
“I call upon them to educate themselves on what is really happening so they will not be victims of disinformation,” he said.

His appeal came amid renewed diplomatic tension after Chinese Ambassador Jing Quan said China could “easily win” if it resorted to force in a confrontation, while maintaining that Beijing preferred peace.

President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. described the ambassador’s remarks as sounding like a threat, while the Department of Foreign Affairs objected to the statement. The government subsequently summoned the Chinese envoy to convey its protest.

In 2016, an arbitral tribunal ruling under the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea rejected China’s expansive claims to historic rights within its so-called nine-dash line where they exceeded the limits allowed under the convention. The ruling is final and binding on both parties, but China has rejected it and continues to dispute the Philippines’ position.
Meanwhile, Burgonio reminded soldiers under his command to remain nonpartisan, warning that violations of military regulations could lead to sanctions.

“So far, there have been no such cases. But if there are, those involved could be sanctioned because that is a blatant violation of our military regulations,” he said, referring to possible instances of partisanship among soldiers.

Burgonio also said the 8ID continues to observe the military chain of command and remains committed to its duties under the leadership of President Marcos, the commander-in-chief, and Defense Secretary Gilberto Teodoro Jr.
He added that the division was not conducting loyalty checks among its personnel, saying soldiers were expected to follow established military regulations and the chain of command./coa

articles.title: 2026 is the year AI is pushed to production
articles.summary: “Two years ago, AI was a demo. Last year, it was a pilot. This year, the leaders who are pulling ahead have moved it into production.” At this year’s VST ECS’ CXO Summit,…

blocks.text: “Two years ago, AI was a demo. Last year, it was a pilot. This year, the leaders who are pulling ahead have moved it into production.”

At this year’s VST ECS’ CXO Summit, President and CEO Jimmy Go laid down the new realities of the AI disruption for Philippine industries. Go tempered optimism with industry challenges. Two years ago, Philippine companies were looking at AI from the lens of curiosity. At last year’s summit, these same companies were piloting AI programs within their own departments or entire organizations. This year, the trend is all about making AI work in order to bring quantifiable gains either in revenue or productivity.

blocks.caption: Jimmy Go President and CEO of VST ECS

blocks.text: AI landscape in the local context

Go cited how the Philippines is making waves in the right direction for AI with data sovereignty, the Pax Silica initiative, and local headways from large hyperscalers like AWS’ USD $5 Billion investment. He also spoke of the Philippine advantage, which is a young population of social media savvy individuals who are the most capable and unafraid of using AI for upskilling.

This also comes at a time where the AI boom has caused pricing to increase drastically, with HBM supply locked until 2027. This has caused a ripple effect with consumer-level smartphones, laptops, and other related technology to increase in pricing by more than 60%.
Measurable AI gains

There have been headwinds made across industries in the Philippines with AI adoption. In the healthcare industry, it’s using predictive AI to discover life-saving molecules within days versus decades. With logistics, it’s about deploying autonomous systems to upgrade or even replace legacy systems. In finance, it’s about using AI to detect fraud by processing millions of micro-transactions.
According to data from VST ECS, there has been a huge shift in enterprise spend and pricing.

For Servers & Storage, allocation shifted heavily toward hyperscalers. Enterprise IT deployments slipped into 2027. Server high-speed DDR5 prices rose nearly 100% quarter on quarter, inflating budgets and delaying smaller enterprise rollouts.

PCs & Notebooks reduced shipments, redesigned configurations, and in some cases downgraded specs. Consumer notebook prices rose 30–50%, with higher costs for midrange models. Smartphones also had rising costs, forcing brands to raise prices or cut shipment targets. IDC projected a 13% drop in global smartphone sales in 2026.

Go’s message to IT decision makers is that despite these fluctuations in the market, in order to remain competitive, you cannot wait for a perfect product to be revealed. As large language models are being improved every month, and memory prices are fluctuating every quarter, it may be tempting to wait. He says that “Waiting for a technology to become perfectly stable before adopting it is a death sentence. By then, others will have already scaled it and captured the advantage. In this era, agility is the real form of risk management.”

articles.title: Musk ordered slowdown of Starlink service used by Ukraine’s military – report
articles.summary: The Wall Street Journal reports Elon Musk and US President Donald Trump discussed the Starlink decision in a call soon after the slowdown became public, while the president was campaigning last week

items: Elon Musk reportedly ordered a slowdown of SpaceX's Starlink service used by Ukraine, impacting their military operations against Russia.
The decision was discussed between Musk and US President Trump, with reports indicating it originated from the White House.
Ukrainian President Zelenskyy is seeking to restore Starlink access amid deteriorating relations with the US, while US officials claim the issue is related to compliance with service terms.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

Elon Musk last week ordered the slowdown of a military-grade version of SpaceX’s Starlink satellite service that Ukraine relies on, the Wall Street Journal reported on Tuesday, October 20, citing US officials and people familiar with the matter.
Musk, SpaceX and the White House did not immediately respond to Reuters requests for comment. Reuters could not immediately verify the report.
Ukraine uses Starlink for battlefield communications and drone operations. Restricting the satellite service hampered the country’s attack and air defense drone missions against Russia.

Musk and US President Donald Trump discussed the Starlink decision in a call soon after the slowdown became public, while the president was campaigning last week, according to the report, which added the two had also discussed the matter prior to the decision to throttle Starlink.
Reuters had reported exclusively that the order to limit the satellite system came from inside the White House.

Trump said last week he did not think either he or Musk was responsible for Ukraine losing Starlink access, while Musk said any limits on speed or Starship or Starshield use were decided by the US military or the president.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy’s relations with Washington have sunk to new lows after Trump announced a deal to buy Russian diesel and waived new sanctions on Moscow. Trump has also told Kyiv to stop attacking Russian refineries and urged Ukrainians to replace Zelenskyy.

Zelenskyy, who is in Oslo in a bid to repair US relations, said on Tuesday he discussed issues including “the situation with Starlink/Starshield, which needs to be restored” with US Secretary of State Marco Rubio.

US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said on Tuesday Washington had not pulled back Ukraine’s ability to access Starlink’s satellite network, but signaled the problem lay with the terms of service Kyiv needed to comply with. – Rappler.com

articles.title: [In This Economy] Marcos’ unconstitutional budgets: Who will answer for them?
articles.summary: The big question is: Will Congress and the Marcos administration account for the affected funds and change how they prepare the next budget?

blocks.text: The Supreme Court has delivered a damning verdict on how Congress and the Marcos administration have handled our national budgets in the past few years.

In a decision announced on Tuesday, October 20, the Supreme Court (SC) declared the 2024 and 2025 General Appropriations Acts (GAAs), or our annual budget laws, unconstitutional. It also struck down two provisions governing the release of unprogrammed appropriations (UA) in the 2026 budget.

This is a historic decision. It’s not every day that the Supreme Court declares GAAs unconstitutional. It also comes on the heels of the SC’s December 2025 decision ordering the return of P60 billion transferred from PhilHealth to the Treasury—done also to fund unprogrammed appropriations.

Note that the Court didn’t invalidate the entire 2026 budget, abolish all unprogrammed appropriations, or order the return of every past payment. Instead, the ruling—dated October 7 and written by Senior Associate Justice Marvic Leonen—exposes serious defects in the way hundreds of billions of pesos were authorized in the past few years.
What went wrong, and what should happen next?

Let’s start with the very concept of unprogrammed appropriations or standby spending authority that the government can use only when specified funding conditions are met. These differ from programmed appropriations, which already form part of the government’s regular spending plan.

In principle, unprogrammed funds can serve legitimate purposes. A foreign-assisted project, for instance, like a railway, may need spending authority contingent on an approved loan. The Supreme Court recognizes that such appropriations can be constitutional.
But just because a spending item is “unprogrammed” doesn’t mean it’s exempted from the Constitution’s budget ceiling. This is a key ruling in the decision.

Article VI, Section 25(1) of our Constitution says Congress may not increase the appropriations recommended by the President for government operations, set yearly in the National Expenditure Program or NEP. For instance, for 2027, the NEP set a P7.2 trillion budget, and Congress cannot exceed that.
What the Supreme Court made clear is that this ceiling should strictly include both programmed and unprogrammed appropriations.

Congress brazenly breached this ceiling in past years. For 2024, the President proposed about P281.9 billion in unprogrammed funds, but Congress raised that to P731.4 billion, amounting to an increase of P449.5 billion or roughly 159%. Hence, the standby allocation became about 2.6 times the original proposal.

The scale of the increase is really mind-boggling. Nearly half a trillion pesos in additional spending authority emerged from the budget legislation process. Programmed appropriations remained unchanged, so the UA increase also raised the combined total above the President’s budget ceiling.

With the 2024 budget ceiling breached, the Supreme Court declared the P449.5-billion increase (and, consequently, the 2024 budget law) unconstitutional. The 2025 budget suffered a similar defect through a P17.992-billion increase in the Department of Public Works and Highways’ Special Road Fund.

From where I sit, the Supreme Court decision is largely a constraint on Congress’ ability to play around with unprogrammed funds. This is the handiwork of Marcos’ allies and family members in Congress, including the former speaker Martin Romualdez (his first cousin), who orchestrated the anomalous budget increases.

But blame rests on the executive, too. President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. and his budget officials—especially former budget secretary Amenah Pangandaman—must explain how budgets with these defects passed through executive scrutiny.

By the way, the ruling also raises questions about the 2023 budget, the Marcos administration’s first, when unprogrammed appropriations reached more than P807 billion. That budget was outside the consolidated cases, however.
Through its recent decision, the Supreme Court also reaffirmed limits on when standby funds can be released.

The challenged 2026 special provisions allowed releases from unprogrammed appropriations when collections from a particular non-tax revenue source exceeded its target, or when a new revenue source produced collections.

Neither condition, by itself, guarantees that total government revenues have exceeded the overall target. The reason is that higher collections from one source—or revenues from a new source—can coexist with larger shortfalls elsewhere.

For instance, suppose the government expects P90 in taxes and P10 from other revenues, for a total of P100. Instead, it collects P80 in taxes and P15 from other sources. There’s a P5 windfall in the second category, but total collections are only P95.
If planned spending is P100, the financing gap is already P5. Authorizing another P5 of spending on the strength of the supposed windfall doubles that gap to P10.

Reaffirming its earlier Araullo ruling, the Supreme Court requires aggregate collections to exceed total revenue targets for the use of unprogrammed appropriations. It invalidated the two triggers found in the 2026 budget, but still allowed approved loans for foreign-assisted projects.

This makes a lot of sense from a fiscal standpoint. Additional spending without genuinely additional resources can mean more borrowing, higher interest costs, or less room for other services. Government borrowing can finance worthwhile investments, but the projects and financing must be assessed in tandem, not in isolation.

The spending of these funds also deserves scrutiny. The decision examines the broadly defined Support for Assistance to Government Infrastructure and Social Programs (SAGIP), which left actual project selection and allocation to the Executive after budget enactment.

Of roughly P200 billion in SAGIP allotment releases in 2024, about P155.9 billion went to public works, including P85.8 billion for flood control. These were authorizations to incur obligations, not proof of completed projects or corruption.

The Supreme Court itself says SAGIP “paved the way for the new pork barrel system.” It recounts the comments of an amicus curiae, UP School of Economics Professor Emerita Solita Monsod, one of my mentors. She explained before the court how infrastructure allocations had become embedded in budget preparation, with lawmakers proposing projects and a “parking fee” allegedly paid for projects outside their districts.
These observations demand investigation: Exactly which allocations financed useful infrastructure, and which financed ghost projects or kickbacks?
The main concern with the ruling is that it does little to recover what was already lost. It’s like shutting the tap after water has already gone down the drain.

A number of lawyer friends immediately pointed out that the Supreme Court applies the doctrine of operative fact, which allows certain consequences of an unconstitutional law to stand when undoing them would unfairly harm people who relied on the law in good faith.

Here, that protection is qualified: it covers irreversible programs, activities, and projects under the affected 2024 unprogrammed appropriations and challenged 2025 accounts, whose beneficiaries relied in good faith on the law’s validity. It doesn’t automatically clear every transaction or protect the officials responsible.

The ruling itself convicts nobody of plunder or graft. Those questions require separate proceedings and proof. But authors, proponents, and implementers of the unconstitutional budget provisions can’t simply invoke the protection of beneficiaries to escape scrutiny.

Moving forward, the Department of Budget and Management (DBM) should publish a project-level accounting of affected funds, distinguishing amounts authorized, released, committed through obligations, and actually paid. Ongoing commitments also need prompt legal review so agencies know which activities can lawfully proceed.

Right now, Congress is finalizing the 2027 budget, and must be guided by the new Supreme Court decision. Specifically, the combined total of programmed and unprogrammed appropriations must stay within the constitutional ceiling.

Congress must also publish a reconciliation of changes to be made by the bicameral conference committee, which settles differences between the House and Senate versions. Every addition should have an identifiable purpose and financing basis.

The Supreme Court ruling is a win not just for budget watchdogs but for Filipinos at large. It gives government an opportunity to correct anomalous practices in recent years. But the big question is: Will Congress and the Marcos administration account for the affected funds and change how they prepare the next budget?

Note, too, that lawmakers wised up and shifted their pork projects away from unprogrammed funds toward programmed funds. The 2027 budget (for the last full year of the Marcos administration, right before the 2028 polls) is shaping up to be as corrupt and patronage-driven as ever.

Pork is here to stay, unless a radical shake-up in the political landscape changes how the budget is crafted and implemented. For Filipinos, bad budgeting is a double-whammy: we’re borrowing and paying for the corrupted amounts they stole from the public coffers. But we get nothing in return by way of quality public goods.
Ang hirap mahalin ng Pilipinas! (It’s hard to love the Philippines!)– Rappler.com

Jan Carlo “JC” Punongbayan, PhD, is an associate professor at the University of the Philippines School of Economics. His professional experience includes the Securities and Exchange Commission, the World Bank Office in Manila, the Far Eastern University Public Policy Center, and the National Economic and Development Authority. JC writes a weekly economics column for Rappler. He is also co-founder of UsapangEcon.com and co-host of Usapang Econ Podcast.

His first book, False Nostalgia: The Marcos “Golden Age” Myths and How to Debunk Them, was published by Ateneo de Manila University Press in February 2023. His second book, Twin Plagues: How Duterte and COVID-19 Wrecked the Philippine Economy, was published by Penguin Random House SEA in June 2026. Follow him on Instagram (@jcpunongbayan).

articles.title: Pangilinan to Marcos: You sent Duterte and Romualdez to jail, you can expel China’s envoy
articles.summary: President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. continues to face pressure from lawmakers to expel China’s ambassador, this time from Sen. Kiko Pangilinan, who reminded him that his government was able to put…

blocks.text: October 21, 2026 | 11:19am
President Marcos accepts the credentials of Chinese Ambassador Jing Quan at Malacañang last December. Looking on is Foreign Affairs Secretary Maria Theresa Lazaro.
Presidential Communications Office

MANILA, Philippines — President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. continues to face pressure from lawmakers to expel China’s ambassador, this time from Sen. Kiko Pangilinan, who reminded him that his government was able to put former President Rodrigo Duterte and his own cousin behind bars.
In a strongly worded statement Tuesday night, Pangilinan challenged the president to take action on the Chinese ambassador.

"Mr. President, if you can send Duterte, Quiboloy and Romualdez to jail, declare POGO illegal and have them shutdown, assert our sovereignty against Chinese aggression then you can most certainly send this arrogant, insulting, crude and insolent alien back to his country of origin," Pangilinan said.
"I have witnessed and thus know that you have what it takes, Mr President. But if you don't use it, you lose it," he said, calling Chinese Ambassador Jing Quan a "hooligan" who should be sent home.

This is Pangilinan's third swipe at the diplomat in days, having previously said the ambassador can "easily leave Manila and go back to China." On Monday, Pangilinan suggested Chinese diplomats who stray from the Communist Party line risk harsh punishment at home.

In the Senate, at least two resolutions have been filed urging the executive branch to consider declaring the Chinese ambassador persona non grata or seek his expulsion. About 10 members of the House of Representatives have separately urged the president to expel Jing, who they say has "clearly overstayed his welcome."

But the Palace itself has been cool to these calls. Palace Press Officer Claire Castro said on Monday that Marcos would not want to have such a declaration for any foreign envoy in the country, though she stressed the Palace respected lawmakers' views.
The DFA has described a persona non grata declaration as a last resort that carries high diplomatic and reciprocal costs.

Neither the Senate nor the House has the power to declare a foreign diplomat persona non grata. This is a power that's only with the executive, specifically the president and the Department of Foreign Affairs (DFA). A sending state however can also recall a diplomat and end their functions.

Jing, after meeting Foreign Affairs Secretary Theresa Lazaro on Monday, released a statement through the Chinese Embassy, saying he has been taken out of context. He accused the Philippine side of committing "smear and slander" against Beijing.

The dispute began on October 15, when Jing, speaking to reporters after a forum in Quezon City, said China would prevail in any armed confrontation but had chosen restraint. "If we want to use force, we may easily win," he said, adding that Manila should count itself lucky to have China as a neighbor.

The DFA answered the same day with a rare public rebuke, saying the remark conveyed a "thinly veiled threat of the use of force." Marcos said the next day it "sounds very much to me like a threat" and that he wanted to hear from Jing what he meant.

articles.title: Guatemalan man gets 30 years for part in smuggling tragedy that killed 53 people in Texas
articles.summary: A U.S. federal judge on Tuesday sentenced a Guatemalan man extradited to the U.S. over his role in a 2022 human smuggling attempt that ended in the deaths of 53 migrants who had been transported in a…

image.caption: Some of the 53 crosses that were part of a makeshift memorial at the site where officials found dozens of people dead in an abandoned trailer containing suspected migrants in 2022. A Guatemalan man was sentenced to 30 years in prison Tuesday for his role in the operation. (Eric Gay/The Associated Pr

blocks.text: World·New

A U.S. federal judge on Tuesday sentenced a Guatemalan man extradited to the U.S. over his role in a 2022 human smuggling attempt that ended in the deaths of 53 migrants who had been transported in a sweltering tractor-trailer in Texas.
The 2022 incident was one of the deadliest human smuggling attempts along the U.S.-Mexico border

U.S. and Guatemalan prosecutors called Rigoberto Ramon Miranda Orozco's sentencing another step toward justice in one of the deadliest smuggling attempts along the U.S.-Mexico border. Miranda Orozco, 50, was sentenced to 30 years in prison after admitting to arranging travel and accommodations for two people who died and another who was seriously injured.

Nearly 20 people in the U.S. and Guatemala have been convicted since the discovery of the abandoned trailer full of bodies horrified communities accustomed to seeing their young people leave, trying to flee poverty or violence in Central America and Mexico.
"It was clear that they suffered tremendously in their last few hours on this earth," U.S. Attorney Justin Simmons told reporters at a news conference following the sentencing.

Police and other first responders work the scene where officials say dozens of people have been found dead and multiple others were taken to hospitals with heat-related illnesses after a semitrailer containing suspected migrants was found, June 27, 2022, in San Antonio, Texas. (Eric Gay/The Associated Press)
People tried to 'claw their way out'

The trailer's air conditioning malfunctioned and would not blow cool air to the people trapped inside during the sweltering, three-hour ride in June 2022 from the border city of Laredo to San Antonio, authorities said. Prosecutors have said migrants paid up to $15,000 US each to be taken across the U.S. border.
When the abandoned trailer was opened on a remote San Antonio back road, 48 migrants were dead. Another 16 were taken to hospitals, where five more died.

items: 46 migrants found dead in abandoned trailer in San Antonio, Texas
Texas migrant deaths: Truck driver among 3 arrested as investigators work to ID dozens of victims

blocks.text: Simmons said investigators found clothing passengers had shed to cool off and claw marks on the trailer's walls.
"They were literally trying to claw their way out," he said.
Twenty-one of those who died were from Guatemala, Simmons said.

Rigoberto Ramon Miranda Orozco, seen here in September 2024, was sentenced to 30 years in prison Tuesday for his role in the 2022 human smuggling case that left 53 migrants dead. (Moises Castillo/The Associated Press)

Miranda Orozco's attorney, Alfonso Cabanas Jr., called the sentence "very tough." He said his client was in Guatemala at the time and had no control over the type of transportation the migrants would take to San Antonio nor did he know the air conditioning was malfunctioning.
Cabanas said he doesn't think harsh punishments will "make a dent" in such operations.
"What we do need is comprehensive immigration reform," Cabanas said.
Other defendants still await sentencing
U.S. District Judge Orlando Garcia sentenced Miranda Orozco, who was arrested in Guatemala in 2024 and extradited to the U.S. the following year.

He pleaded guilty in July to conspiracy to bring a migrant into the U.S. resulting in death, aiding and abetting bringing a migrant into the U.S. resulting in death, as well as aiding and abetting bringing a migrant into the U.S. resulting in serious bodily injury, prosecutors said.

Simmons said prosecutors in Guatemala were integral in securing convictions for Miranda Orozco and others. Simmons was joined by Guatemalan Attorney General Gabriel García Luna, who reflected on the suffering the migrants inside the tractor-trailer endured.
"They paid for a promise, and those who cashed in on that promise abandoned them to their fate," García Luna said.

Last year, Felipe Orduna-Torres, described by prosecutors as the leader of the smuggling operations inside the U.S., was sentenced to life in prison in the U.S. Armando Gonzales-Ortega, his top assistant, was sentenced to 83 years.
More sentencing dates to come

The tragedy is the deadliest among those that have claimed thousands of lives in recent decades as people attempt to cross the U.S. border from Mexico. Ten migrants died in 2017 after they were trapped inside a truck parked at a Walmart in San Antonio.
In 2003, the bodies of 19 migrants were found in a sweltering truck southeast of San Antonio.

articles.title: De Lima: SC limiting use unprogrammed appropriations prevents abuse of public funds
articles.summary: The Supreme Court decision restricting the use of unprogrammed appropriations (UA) and prohibiting Congress from increasing budgets above the President's proposal has shut the door for abuse in…

blocks.text: Published October 21, 2026 11:03am

The Supreme Court decision restricting the use of unprogrammed appropriations (UA) and prohibiting Congress from increasing budgets above the President's proposal has shut the door for abuse in spending public funds, House Senior Deputy Minority Leader Leila de Lima of Mamamayang Liberal (ML) party-list said Wednesday.

De Lima was referring to the Supreme Court (SC) decision declaring as illegal the 2024 and 2025 national budgets and provisions of 2026 budget on unprogrammed allocations due to congressional increases that went beyond the budget ceiling as proposed by the President.

"The Supreme Court's decision on Unprogrammed Appropriations (UA) is a significant win in our fight for transparency and accountability in spending the people's money. The Court ruled that the UA can have no lump sums and that new revenues should presumptively fund programmed expenditures. Where there is more than one purpose, Congress must establish sufficient standards in terms of prioritization for spending, and the UA must remain what it was always meant to be: a narrow contingent appropriation," she said in a statement.

The Supreme Court's decision partially granted the petition filed by De Lima and Caloocan 2nd District Representative Edgar Erice challenging the constitutionality of Chapter XLIII of the 2026 GAA, which authorized unprogrammed appropriations.

In the decision, the SC ruled that "Unprogrammed Appropriations are not unconstitutional per se," but stressed that these need "clear limits and safeguards to preserve fiscal discipline, transparency, and accountability."

De Lima said, "As a co-petitioner in one of the consolidated cases, we had hoped that the Court would abolish the UA entirely, as we believe that it is tantamount to undue delegation of legislative power to the Executive and that prudent budget does not need a standing reserve for discretion. Still, we thank the SC for setting clear constitutional limits on UA–a big step toward promoting fiscal discipline and pursuing a coherent fiscal program. UA was meant to be a standby, not a slush fund. The Court has put it back in its proper place."
De Lima then said the court ruling is a warning against those who will sneak in to misuse public funds.

The high bench also voided the 2024 budget because of a P449.5-billion increase in unprogrammed appropriations, while the 2025 GAA was struck down because of the additional P17.99 billion for the Special Road Fund of the Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH).

Meanwhile, Senator Panfilo "Ping" Lacson on Wednesday said the Supreme Court ruling came at an opportune time as the Senate scrutinizes the House version of the proposed 2027 national budget. — VDV, GMA News

articles.title: Elon Musk ordered a slowdown of Starlink in Ukraine — report

blocks.text: Tech billionaire Elon Musk ordered the slowdown of a military-grade version of SpaceX's Starlink satellite service that Ukraine relies on, the Wall Street Journal reported on Tuesday, citing US officials.
Kyiv uses Starlink for battlefield communications and drone operations. Restricting the service means restricting the country's attack and defense missions against Russia.

Last week, Musk capped the speeds at which Ukrainian hardware could stay connected to the satellite-based network, the report said citing unnamed sources. The move rendered some offensive drones and interceptor drones virtually useless, it added.
Two people told the Journal that Musk and US President Donald Trump discussed the Starlink decision in a call, soon after the slowdown became public.

Some US officials, the report said, believed Musk acted unilaterally and that Trump did not specifically order retribution against Ukraine. However, one person familiar with the situation said Musk talked to multiple senior administration officials, including Trump, even before imposing the speed limitation.
Both Musk and Trump have expressed anger at Ukraine for attacking Russian diesel refineries in recent weeks, which the president blames for high energy prices.
The report also comes after Trump's comments last week that he did not think either he or Musk was responsible for Ukraine losing Starlink access.
Musk had said that any limits on speed or use were decided by the US military or the president.
Musk, SpaceX, and the White House are yet to respond to the report.
